1.	What are the standards by which the salaries of postmaster and assistant postmaster are established?
2.	Do these standards apply to the whole of Canada?
3.	Does the Minimum Wage Act apply to the Post Office Department?

4.	If not, what category of employees is not covered by this act and why?

1.	The classification of Post Offices is based on the volume of postal business transacted. The salaries of the Postmasters and Assistants are based on the classification thus determined.
2.	Yes.
3.	The Minimum Wage Acts of Provincial Governments do not apply to Post Office Department employees. The Government, as a matter of policy, has established that minimum wage standards within the Canada Labour (Standards) Code would be extended to Federal Government employees.
The Civil Service Regulations have been amended with respect to annual vacation, general holidays and a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour to conform with the conditions outlined in the Code and these new regulations apply to Post Office Department employees who are subject to the terms of the Civil Service Act. They do not apply to small Revenue Postmasters and Sub Postmasters.
4.	Revenue Postmasters are paid on the basis of postal work performed rather than on time required to be available to provide service. They are available to provide service for 40 hours per week but they may engage in other gainful employment when not required for postal work. Many of them operate stores in conjunction with the Post Office and where the Post Office is located in a home, there is little interference with the performance of normal household activities. On the basis of the hours required to perform postal work, they are paid in excess of the minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. Sub-Post Offices are usually operated in conjunction with another business and, like Revenue Offices, Postmasters are not required to devote full-time to postal work. They are paid a basic amount plus commissions on the sale of postal values. The status of these two groups in so far as the application of the Labour Code is concerned is still under review.

April 20, 1966

speakeroldname: Hon. Roberi Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CORRELATION OF FAIRS, ETC. AND EXPO '67
speechtext:
A very active program is in progress to promote Expo '67 at major Canadian fairs and exhibitions. It is the intention to have prominent displays at the Calgary Stampede, the Pacific National exhibition and the Canadian National exhibition. Expo '67 will be participating jointly with the Ontario government at the Canadian National exhibition, and at other fairs and exhibitions across Canada. All Expo '67 exhibits will include reference to its role in the Canadian centennial.
In addition, Expo '67 and the centennial commission are co-operating in several major national projects: (a) one which will result in national and international performing groups playing in several major centres of Canada as well as at Expo '67; (b) a series of folk art festivals; (c) the youth travel program under which hundreds of Canadian students will be assisted in travelling to various parts of Canada, some of whom may visit at Expo '67 when going through Montreal; (d) the canoe pageant; (e) a centennial guide book and the Canadian armed forces tattoo.
These and other events are described in the third annual report of the centennial commission for the fiscal year 1964-65.

The Canadian Federation of University Women recommended that salary paid to a wife employed by her husband (or a partnership in which he is a member) be treated as separate income in the wife's hands when the services are actually performed and the compensation is not greater than would be paid to another person for the same services.
The Canadian Federation of Business and Professional Women's Clubs urged that subsections (2) and (3) of section 21 of the Income Tax Act be repealed and that the act be amended to provide that where the service is actually performed and the compensation is not greater than would be paid to another person for the same service the remuneration received by the employee spouse shall be deductible from the taxable income of the employer spouse, and shall be treated as separate income in the hands of the employee spouse.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce recommended that remuneration received by an employed spouse be treated as separate to the extent that services are actually performed and the compensation is not greater than would be paid to an unrelated person for the same service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
1. The terminated 1946 Canada-United Kingdom income tax agreement has been renegotiated in part and replaced by a limited agreement, signed on December 6, 1965, that deals with four classes of income.
Both governments have expressed the hope that the limited agreement will soon be extended to include the subjects usually covered in a comprehensive agreement, and arrangements are now being made for holding meetings with a view to negotiating such an agreement.
2.	The limited agreement will not be ratified by an exchange of instruments of ratification but will come into force after each contracting government has been notified by the other that all the things that have to be done to give the agreement the force of law in Canada and the United Kingdom respectively have been done. The governing date is expected to be the date on which the Canadian bill to implement the agreement is given royal assent.
It cannot now be determined when any comprehensive agreement that may be negotiated will come into force.
3.	Yes, with respect to the subjects covered in the limited agreement. Not known, with respect to the subjects to be covered in any comprehensive agreement that may be negotiated.
4.	Yes. The Income Tax Act provides that residents of Canada are taxable on income from all sources; it also provides that tax credits shall be allowed in respect of taxes paid to foreign governments on income from foreign sources.

Are any controls, regulations or legislation at present in effect in Canada to ensure that federal moneys extended to the provinces on a cost-sharing Stasis for technical school development programs are used for this specific purpose and, if so, what are they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Yes. Control over the uses to which federal contributions toward technical and vocational training projects and programs are put by the provinces is exercised through the provisions of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act and the technical and vocational training and apprenticeship training agreements made thereunder with the provinces. The act and the agreements authorize federal contributions to be made only in respect of costs or expenditures incurred by the provinces for purposes specified therein. The act describes these purposes in general terms; the agreements describe them in detail and also make provision for individual approval of capital expenditure and certain other projects by the minister or administrators of his department. The agreements further require that the provinces maintain full records of all expenditures and commitments made as well as revenues and refunds received in respect of such agreements, and that the provinces permit access to such records, documents and files as may be deemed necessary by the comptroller of the treasury, the Auditor General of Canada, or other authorized officers of the federal government for the audit of expenditure under the agreements.

Did the Prime Minister make a statement in Calgary in October, 1965, in regard to National Parks policy and, if so, what was that statement?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Yes. Such a statement was included in my speech at the Palliser hotel in Calgary on October 20, 1965, during the election campaign. Following is an extract from the transcript of what I said:
There is another matter worrying you out here, and I understand you are worried, and that is that we are interfering in the administration of public parks in a way which will violate the rights of certain people who have vested interest in those parks. I understand this worry and anxiety and I have written one of our candidates who is particularly concerned with this, and I would like to read what wrote him, and this is a week or so ago.
I said: "I want to dispel this anxiety. There will be full opportunity for park residents and others concerned to make their views known before any final decision is taken by government". And I repeat that. I am glad to give that pledge. "In many cases" I said, "there are difficulties in reconciling the long term interests of Canadians generally"-and we have a responsibility in the federal government for the interests of Canadians generally and their interests in public parks-"the difficulty of reconciling that with the legitimate rights of individuals who have acquired very specific interests, such as leaseholds in the parks. It is not easy to solve such problems to the satisfaction of all concerned but every effort will be made to do this, and to this end the government will give careful consideration to the views of all those who are concerned, before deciding what further action it should take in the light of the provisions laid down by parliament in the National Parks Act".
I hope this commitment on my part will remove some of the understandable anxiety that is felt.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the Minister of Finance on his first budget speech, both as to its presentation and content. The amendment before us is obviously an attempt, a very hard attempt, to find something that is wrong with something that is very good and a budget that is very much required for the very tricky economic conditions that we have in Canada today. I want to devote the whole of my speech to considering that budget in the light of the four western provinces of Canada. I make no apology for speaking on behalf of the four western provinces, the fastest growing and most exciting provinces of Canada.
During the course of the minister's speech he referred to the question of tariff policy for Canada and the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations being sponsored by the members
4072	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Basford of GATT. The Kennedy round seems to me to have almost become bogged down in a round of endless negotiation and discussion and, as the Minister of Finance very rightly warned us, the powers accorded the United States government by the U.S. Trade Expansion Act expire in 1967.
I know the minister will give every impetus to our Canadian negotiations to assure that the Kennedy round is as successful as possible in causing multilateral reductions of tariffs and the creation of freer and more liberal trade. The minister said in his speech, as reported at page 3376 of Hansard:
But at a time when we are engaged in one of the largest international tariff negotiations in our history I think the house will appreciate the desirability of using whatever tariff reductions we contemplate to help us obtain better access to foreign markets for our own exports.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
With that statement, Mr. Speaker, I am in general agreement, particularly when we look at our markets in Europe and the United States. However, I should like to draw the minister's attention to one area of the world to which I think this tariff program is not necessarily applicable, namely, the numerous so-called Pacific rim areas, Japan and the underdeveloped areas of Southeast Asia. I suggest that to have access for Canadian products to these markets it is not necessary for us to engage in bilateral tariff negotiations. We in Canada have traditionally been oriented to our Atlantic and European markets. This suggestion is not new with me. Our trading policy in Canada must also be oriented to the vast potential markets of the Pacific ocean area. Access to these markets for Canada, unlike our traditional markets, is not so dependent upon international tariff negotiations.
To gain access to this area we would not have to engage in bilateral or multilateral tariff negotiations. I suggest they play a minor part, and rather more important is that our foreign policy generally and our foreign aid and credit policy specifically must be complementary to our trading policy. As an export market for the raw materials, the mineral concentrates, potash-I compliment the minister for removing the tax on potash extraction-chemicals, the wheat and grain products of western Canada, we do not believe that eastern Canada and the Atlantic community provide the answer but we look rather across the ocean to Japan, southeast Asia and western Latin America.

DEBATES	April 20. 1966
We on the west coast are bordering on one of the most populous regions of the world. As the underdeveloped Asian countries develop, their need for raw materials and manufactured products will be immense. In western Canada we want to assure that Canada fills a high proportion of those needs.
Surely it is in Canada's interest to do everything possible to realize the potentials of trading into this area. In order to do so we must undertake a realignment of some of our traditional trading patterns, and I want to make three specific recommendations. We have, as stressed by the minister, a difficult and dangerous balance of payments problem with the United States which must be solved. In referring to longer term solutions to our balance of payments problem the minister said, as reported on page 3379 of Hansard:
Our basic approach is twofold; first, through industrial, commercial and manpower policies, to adapt the structure of the Canadian economy to exploit effectively the most rapidly growing markets at home and abroad;
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I almost wish he had said we would use industrial, commercial, manpower, water and transportation policies to adapt the structures of the Canadian economy to exploit all of these markets. It certainly seems to me, at this particular time, that it is idle chatter to discuss the export and sale of western Canadian water which is going to be needed in the four western provinces for the agricultural and industrial development of western Canada.
I suggest that possibly the most rapidly growing markets abroad are in industrial Japan and the developing nations of southeast Asia. I suggest to the minister that many of the products we now buy from the United States, and which contribute to our balance of payments problem, could well be bought from Japan, a country with which we have an overwhelmingly favourable balance of trade. I should like to quote briefly from the Journal of Commerce, an important western publication for March 26, 1966, in which the changing pattern of Pacific trade is discussed. The Journal said:
These products are finding an increasingly important place-
Referring to the new products coming from Japan.
-in western Canadian markets. They range from motorcycles and automobiles to heavy tractors; from small upright drills to large turret lathes; from insulators to electric generators; from steel plate to huge diameter pipe.
April 20, 1966

At the same time, Japan has become an important market for Canadian raw materials, as well as finished and semi-finished goods. Japanese industry is teaming up with Canadian investors to explore and develop many resources, thereby putting mines, pulp mills and other industries here into full production.
In 1964, Mr. Speaker, only 9 per cent of Canada's textile imports came from Japan, only 4 per cent of our sundries came from the same source and Japan supplied only 2.3 per cent of our total Canadian imports. Even in view of these surprisingly low figures and our continuously favourable trade balance with Japan as well as our dangerous imbalance with the United States, Japan is asked to impose upon itself voluntary quotas on its exports to Canada. I suggest that this is principally in order to allow some of our marginal and often antiquated industries to continue to struggle along.
Canada's trade with Japan last year amounted to $350 million in exports and $220 million in imports, leaving a trade balance in our favour of $130 million. These are the latest available 1965 estimates. In line with the minister's policy announcement of taking industrial, commercial and manpower policies to exploit effectively the most rapidly growing markets abroad, and since Japan is one of those markets, I recommend to him in the strongest possible terms the immediate removal of voluntary quotas on Japanese imports to Canada and the removal of other tariff impediments to Japanese trade. Japanese-Canadian trade, Mr. Speaker, is good for Canada. We should remove immediately any impediments to that trade.
As a second specific recommendation, it seems to me that many of our industrial and commercial concerns are afraid of the impact upon their business of the importation of products from abroad without tariff protection. It is trite to say that trade is a two way street and in order to sell we must buy. It is understandable that the owners of businesses which will be affected by increased importations, and the workers in those industries, would be concerned about the future and security of their capital or of their jobs.
I think that we in Canada have not yet developed the proper techniques for dealing with this problem. President Kennedy's trade expansion act, which was designed to provide a lowering of United States tariffs and to bring about increased imports into the United States, provided machinery by which the government could assist those industries and
The Budget-Mr. Basford those jobs affected by lower tariffs. I recommend to the minister that we in Canada must also develop similar techniques. In recommending increased imports from Japan, for example, I am not unmindful of the problems, or at least the concern, created, for example, in the Canadian textile industry. We must develop machinery to assist those people who would be affected or who think they would be affected.
This government's labour mobility program and other programs, for which I compliment them in that they are new, imaginative programs, will be of some help in this connection. However, I believe we must go farther than the existing policies in assisting the relocation of capital and of jobs that will be affected by freer trade. We need newer techniques to eliminate the understandable human concern of some people for the future of their business or of their jobs. We need also a policy directly aimed at assisting capital and workers in moving from one productive process to another.
Third, Mr. Speaker, in order to develop our export markets to the fullest it is essential that we develop transportation policies and facilities that can get the products of western Canada to those markets of the Pacific Ocean area speedily, cheaply and on guaranteed delivery schedules. On December 13 last year the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) announced an integrated study of Atlantic provinces transportation problems. I should like to quote from the press release of that date:
The integrated study of transportation problems and requirements of the Atlantic provisions was officially launched...
Acres Research and Planning Limited... will combine forces with the Economist Intelligence Unit of London, England, to carry out this major transportation study...
The over-all objective of the study is to assess the effectiveness of the present transportation systems and to determine how they can best be developed to foster the economic growth and wellbeing of the Atlantic provinces.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Farther on there is this statement:
Adequate transportation links between the Atlantic provinces and the major economic areas of the continent are essential to the growth of these provinces. Rising production and consumption are reflected in greater traffic flows. It is recognized that existing networks of road, rail, air and water transportation will have to be improved and extended. This may require major revisions involving considerable capital expenditure. The Atlantic provinces' transportation study will review the transportation problems against the background of the prospects for growth in the primary and secondary industries of all four provinces.
April 20. 1966

The Budget

Mr. Basford
The Atlantic Development Board, the government of Canada and the premiers of the four Atlantic provinces have seen the need and the wisdom of such a study for the Atlantic provinces. I suggest and specifically recommend that if Canada is to exploit its foreign markets to the fullest such a study is urgently required for the four western provinces.
The rapidly rising export from western Canada of grain, metal concentrates, potash, gypsum, sulphur and chemicals has already led to transportation problems, bottlenecks and lack of facilities. We need only recall the debate on box cars in this house not so many weeks ago. This situation seriously limits or endangers many of our overseas transactions, and I suggest that in the future it will become even more serious.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I propose that there should be a comprehensive analysis of all of the transportation, storage and handling systems which are or will be involved in moving and distributing western Canadian resources and products to inland and overseas customers. The specific objectives of the proposed study should be to develop recommendations on a short, medium and long term basis to lead to actions to (a) increase western Canada's capacity for transporting its products to local and overseas customers; (b) increase the speed of our deliveries; (c) increase the reliability of our deliveries, and (d) reduce to the lowest possible level the costs of delivery to keep our products competitive.
Such a study would involve a review and analysis of western Canada's future sales and potential market areas over the next 15 to 25-year period and a determination of our transportation requirements to fulfil these maximum sales and reach these market areas. It would involve, therefore, a careful review and analysis of all of the links in our transportation chain, a study of our local and pool elevators, a study of our present and future extractive resource sites, the future sites of mines, refineries and pulp mills, our rail operations including both their possible abandonment and curtailment and also, more importantly, their development into new resource areas, the economy and efficiency of unit trains for the movement of bulk cargo, a study of the capacity of the Fraser Canyon rail lines and methods of increasing that capacity by either twinning the tracks or using one track eastbound and the other westbound.

This review and analysis would also involve a study of our trucking operations, both as a means of delivery to intermediate or final loading points, and the need for and best location of a second trans-Canada highway; the place of fluid pipe lines and, even more exciting, the role of solids pipe lines for the transportation of coal, chemicals and even grain, on which the Alberta Research Council and others have already done such valuable work; inland shipping, direct ocean shipping; the terminal, storage, transfer and handling facilities of our Pacific ports of Vancouver, New Westminster and Prince Rupert for both general cargo and, probably more importantly, bulk loading facilities; the examination of new port sites such as the presently discussed Sturgeon Banks off the lower mainland of British Columbia, and our Pacific port handling facilities not only for today's vessels but for the type of vessels that will be arriving, or at least should be arriving, on the Pacific coast in the future.
Each part of our western transportation system, Mr. Speaker, both publicly and privately owned, should be studied to determine and assess its present capacity, operation and effectiveness and the extent and speed with which the capacity and effectiveness of each facility can and should be increased. We should determine the bottlenecks and inadequacies of our transportation system and the sequence in which these bottlenecks should be eliminated or the inadequacies filled.
The Atlantic transportation study which I mentioned is being conducted by Acres Research and Planning Limited in consortium with the Economist Intelligence Unit of London, England, and I am sure there are other firms working either singly or in consortium which would be suitable for such a study of western Canadian transportation.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, another full-dress royal commission on transportation facilities; in fact, I would deplore the appointment of such. As an aside I might almost say: God preserve us from the present ones we have working. I want and I am advocating rather a comprehensive and coordinated study, by knowledgeable and expert consulting engineers and transportation and market analysts, of our transportation needs in western Canada both present and future and how best our transportation systems, co-ordinated on an economic and feasible basis, can foster the economic growth,
April 20, 1966	COMMONS
prosperity and development of the four western provinces.
Such consultants as I am advocating should divide their recommendations into short-term, medium-term and long-term proposals so that within one or at the most two years recommendations and action plans could be designed for a group of immediate improvements. Then during subsequent stages of the examination, over say three to five years, longer term recommendations could be devised and a continuing analysis of the implementation of previously approved recommendations could be made.
In the time allowed to me, Mr. Speaker, I have recommended three specific things in connection with the increasing and total exploitation of the markets which are available to the products of western Canada. I have suggested the removal of voluntarily imposed quotas on Japan and the removal of all tariff impediments to Canadian-Japanese trade. I have suggested policies to assist those industries and workers which would be affected by freer trade so that they would not oppose the liberalization or freeing of our trade. Third, I have recommended transportation policies so that western Canada can maximize its endeavours to gain access to the markets of the Pacific ocean area. These are specific proposals, Mr. Speaker.
In conclusion may I say to the Minister of Finance in a general way, and I know he is not unsympathetic to this view, that in working out his budgetary proposals for this country and in shaping the fiscal, tariff and monetary policies of Canada he must always remind himself that we live in a very vast country composed of five quite different economic regions, the interests of which are not always compatible and sometimes conflict. He must also remind himself, and I emphasize this, that that which is good for central Canada is not necessarily always good for the extremities of the country, such as the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia, and also the prairies. Yet the extremities of the country both east and west, the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia, and also the prairies, have a right to look and must be able to look to him as minister and to the government of Canada to initiate policies which will assist, foster and strengthen the industrial, commercial and trade development of the far eastern and far western regions of Canada.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss today a national resource before I discuss generally the provisions of the budget. My remarks are directed specifically to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who I am very happy to see is in his seat, and to the government. My remarks, sir, are directed as well to all members of this house and also to you.
There is some misunderstanding, I believe, with respect to a matter I raised on one or two occasions in the house before the Easter recess with respect to the pilfering by commercial organizations in the city of Edmonton of the Klondike theme.
There can be no doubt about the responsibility of the government of Canada for the development of northern resources. There can be no doubt about the exclusiveness of the jurisdiction of the government of Canada over the development of these resources. It follows, therefore, that there is a direct responsibility on the minister and on the government in the resource development field. Unlike the provinces where exclusive jurisdiction over resource development resides entirely within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, the responsibility here is clearly that of the government and of the minister.
I therefore suggest, sir, that when the matter is raised in the house, and when I make these remarks I cast no reflections whatsoever upon the Chair, I am merely endeavouring to inform the Chair of the national nature of the subject matter which has been raised by me on previous occasions, on each occasion that the matter is raised it must be determined whether it is one of sufficient urgency to be raised on orders of the day.
It is also quite clear, sir, that tourism is a resource. The extent to which tourist revenues in this country increased under the previous government to a point where for the first time in history our balance of trade with the United States was on the credit side is a matter of record.
There is also, sir, no doubt that throughout the whole world the romantic ring of the Klondike remains despite the passage of 68 years. The Klondike and all that that era stands for remains in the minds of people throughout the world. It is a great tourist drawing card. It is a potential tourist revenue earner in an industry the development of
April 20, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen which is vital to bringing the Yukon out of what the minister himself has described as a deficit area.
That the Klondike is in the Yukon can also not be doubted. That the whole of the Yukon tourist industry is built around the Klondike is also quite clear. Any extended effort, therefore, by any agency whatsoever to attempt to drain off by the exploitation of the Klondike theme tourist revenues from the Yukon will seriously impair not only the development of that industry in the Yukon but will also seriously impair that day when the Yukon can call itself economically independent and that day when the Yukon can look forward, because of that fact, to selfgovernment.
I am sure that the commercial organizations in the city of Edmonton and the city fathers were well meaning in choosing the theme of the development days of the Klondike when three years ago, I believe, the federal government evidenced a declining interest in the promotion of several projects in which the government of Canada had invested substantially. The Yukon had been developing its Klondike tourist industry for many years before the city of Edmonton commenced what I have called on previous occasions this larcenous exploitation of a resource which in no way belongs to it.
It would be different if this exploitation were a one-night stand. It would be different if it were on isolated occasions that the theme was exploited. It has been exploited in almost every province and in many cities and communities throughout Canada; in fact, it has been exploited not only in Canada but throughout the world. However, this is an extended and continuing effort by the city of Edmonton with, I must assume, the condonation of the province of Alberta to exploit something to which they have absolutely no proprietary right.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you saying there are a lot of bootleggers?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are claim jumpers. That is what they are. This continuing exploitation, sir, is hitting the Yukon hard. The minister will agree with that. It is syphoning off tourist revenues that otherwise would go to the Yukon. The argument is, of course, that we are adopting a dog in the manger attitude.
Sir, we do not have the resources in the Yukon that the city of Edmonton has within its municipal boundaries in order to fully

exploit this resource. Our efforts must be combined and are being combined with those of the previous government and this government to exploit this resource for the benefit of the economic future of the Yukon. Many tourists the world over under the impact of the tremendous publicity campaign now being carried on by the city of Edmonton will stay in Edmonton, enjoy the Klondike days which have been organized there and go home thinking they have seen the Klondike. The result will be a distortion of Canadian history.
The Klondike is not in Edmonton, nor does that famous and fabulous era of Canadian history have anything to do with Edmonton. It was not Edmonton that made the contribution in the way the Klondike did to the over-all economic development of this country during the gold rush days.
The promotional literature I hold in my hand, sir, is an expensive, coloured brochure issued by the Edmonton Exhibition Association and it leaves the clear impression that the Klondike is in the city of Edmonton. They have stolen Klondike Mike. They have stolen Klondike Kate. They have stolen the Chilkoot mine. They have even stolen the Yukon.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is hard.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has in large print: "Ride The E.Y. & P." Then in small print it says:
A small version of the famous Edmonton, Yukon & Pacific steam train chugs and hisses around the half mile-
And so it goes.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is still in Edmonton.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The White Pass and Yukon route is the railway of history that chugged its way through the days of the Klondike gold rush.
Another advertisement says that you can visit the Chilkoot mine of those famous days, even though very few Edmontonians involved in this commercial exploitation know the geographic location of the Chilkoot pass. It is said that you can pan for real gold nuggets. Well, sir, they would have to be imported because there are none in Edmonton.
Under the heading, "Lively Downtown Celebrations", is the following:
Local citizens wear costumes of the Klondike era-recalling the fabulous excitement of the gold rush era.
April 20, 1966

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
When did Edmonton have a gold rush era? They like to say, sir, that many prospectors and sourdoughs who travelled to the Yukon passed through Edmonton. Sir, the cities of Seattle, San Francisco and Vancouver played a much larger part in that history than the city of Edmonton ever did. In another part of this brochure they invite the citizens to "return to the lively days of the gold rush." Again, this is in the city of Edmonton. How can we in the Yukon compete with the Mounted Police musical ride which has been imported for the purpose of this immoral and illegal exploitation? I am surprised that the Mounted Police would lend themselves to such an unlawful purpose and I mean no reflection on the force when I say this. "Bonanza", too, has been stolen. Under all this material we find the inscription of the Edmonton Exhibition Association whose motto is printed here as being "Pro Bono Publico", for the public good.
It does a disservice to Canada to allow this kind of exploitation to continue. Neither the citizens of the Yukon nor the government of the Yukon can endorse a continuance of this kind of illegal and immoral exploitation. When I say "the government of the Yukon" I mean the minister and his representative in the Yukon together with the Yukon legislative council. I believe the minister has received a resolution passed unanimously by the Yukon legislative council asking him to take action. The government of the province of Alberta cannot be left out because we are not speaking of the Yukon versus Edmonton in this issue; we are speaking of the Yukon and the province of Alberta. We can no more speak of the Yukon and Edmonton than we can of Dawson and Edmonton. I suggest to the minister that he has an obligation to act, and to act now, on the request of the people of the Yukon made known to him through the Yukon legislative council. He has an even greater responsibility. It is to retain intact a resource which comes under his personal protection as a member of a government which has direct responsibility for resource development.
The council has asked the minister to intervene with the government of the province of Alberta. It has asked for his intervention with the city of Edmonton. It has asked for his intervention with those responsible for Expo '67. Instead of allowing the city of Edmonton to anticipate the establishment of any kind of display at Expo '67 which would

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen involve the exploitation of the Klondike, the minister should himself be considering taking action at Expo '67 similar to that which was taken during the last Grey Cup parade. He advertised the Yukon in that parade, and quite properly. He should take the same attitude now and give this matter his most serious consideration.

speechtext: Would the hon. member be agreeable to calling it "the real Klondike"?

There is only one legitimate Klondike. Anything less than that is a hoax. Anything less than that is an immoral if not an illegal offer made by agencies so as to deprive an area coming under the minister's direct responsibility of its proprietary right to a resource the responsibility for the development of which lies upon the hon. gentleman's shoulders.
That legal action is possible should not escape the minister's consideration. I ask him to look at section 306 of the Criminal Code which deals specifically with frauds of this nature.

I have, sir. We in the Yukon are ready to believe that those who originated this exploitation did so in a well meaning fashion. But we also believe they do not appreciate the serious and deleterious long range effect this kind of thing will have on the development not only of this specific resource but of the Yukon as a whole. We asked them to reconsider that poster. This is not a dog in a manger attitude we are taking. Many thousands of taxpayers' dollars out of Canadian pockets generally have gone into the building up and exploitation of the tourist resource in the north. Our tourist resource in this part of northern Canada, the Yukon, is built solidly, squarely, specifically and exclusively on the Klondike area. Any attempt to mislead tourists into believing that the Klondike area exists elsewhere is bald fraud.
As to the Budget generally, I have studied this Budget trying to find a clue to a coherent fiscal or economic policy, and I can say it makes trying to find a needle in a haystack an absolute cinch. They took the tax off false teeth. After the new taxes no one will need their teeth, false or otherwise. At present food prices teeth are a waste of time.
April 20, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen
A serious question affecting mortgages was raised today by my right hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). The minister in charge of housing, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), said today

I believe I heard him correctly-that the problem was nation-wide and had become so in the last few weeks. This can be attributed directly to the policies of the present government outlined in the Budget and to the ruinous acceptance by this administration of guide lines emanating from Washington.
While I am referring to the Minister of Labour I am compelled to add that he is the Only minister now in charge of a skeleton department. Some have skeleton staffs but the Minister of Labour has a skeleton department. In this connection I should refer in passing to the report on the Department of Labour by Woods, Gordon and Company dated November, 1965, in which it is stressed that manpower and labour relations must be closely integrated. This government completely ignored that report in setting up a separate department of manpower. Here is a massive survey undertaken at a great deal of public expense and completed no later than November last. Yet immediately after the election it is thrown out of the window for reasons of pure expediency.
I submit that the Budget tackled inflation at the wrong end. The problem of inflation is to equate production with demand. Hon. gentlemen opposite are cutting down demand instead of helping production. Canadians are being penalized in an era of plenty because this government has no confidence in the capacity of the economy to produce enough to meet demand.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Canadian industry and Canadian labour can produce. There can be no doubt on that score. The real problem confronting us today is that costs of production have risen. Why have costs of production gone up? They have gone up because the cost of everything the working man must buy has gone out of sight. Never before in the history of this country have we had not only such a high cost of living but, over a few short years, such a remarkably accelerated increase in that cost of living. The costs of food, clothing, recreation and accommodation have soared. Food costs alone went up 7 per cent in the past year. The result is that labour has been forced to ask for higher wages in order to make ends meet. No one can blame labour for that. People who work for a living have a 
right to a fair share of the present prosperity but under this government, with high taxes, high prices and high costs, this has been denied.
Why do we have high prices? It is because the government increased the money supply in Canada by 12 per cent in 1965 compared with 6 per cent in 1964.

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen
What the government should have done was to remove immediately the 11 per cent sales tax on equipment and material in order to reduce costs to industry. Instead it has promised to cut it down to 6 per cent in April, 1967, and to remove it by 1968. This, I suggest, is too little and too late.
What has happened is that the Budget completely failed to take into consideration the real needs of Canada's economy. We must maintain, not curb, expansion. We must do it without allowing inflation to continue unchecked. The minister's approach was purely that of a bureaucrat eager to cure the symptoms without considering the real nature of the disease. There is a very real possiblity that the shortsighted and negative approach in the Budget will endanger Canada's economic expansion and place this nation's economy in a strait-jacket. Already there are signs of that happening.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is a government, sir, which gives the appearance of fearing expansion. A timid, fearful and negative attitude is the very antithesis to what is required at the present time. We must preserve the prosperity which Canadians have worked so hard to achieve and at the same time maintain a reasonable balance between costs and prices. We must remove taxes which serve only to hinder and not encourage the smooth flow of economic expansion.
As a Conservative I am particularly concerned about the effects of this negative and overly-cautious approach, because it was our policies which made prosperity possible; it was our policies which enabled the ex-minister of finance to say that the upswing in the economy began in 1961, which I do not believe the minister will dispute.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Was it not the policies of the previous administration which brought about the exchange crisis?

It certainly was not. It certainly was not this party which did such a disservice to Canada's image internationally as was done by those now occupying the treasury benches in their political campaigns in 1962 and 1963 by disparaging the devaluation of the dollar, a situation that the minister now has no intention of altering. A great thing has happened as a result of the devaluation of the dollar; yet the minister and those surrounding him in those election

campaigns certainly were the severest critics of the action taken at that time.

And in so doing did a great disservice to Canada's image internationally.
The present expansion, as the minister knows, is now in its fifth year having begun in 1961, two years before the Liberal government took office. It commenced as a result of, first, the massive wheat sales, wheat sales that were strongly criticized from across the way when that policy was announced by the previous government. It began as a result of capital development programs such as the Saskatchewan dam and the Pine Point railroad, which again were severely criticized by those opposite when they sat on this side of the house.
Another factor in the expansion was the assistance to shipbuilding, seriously curtailed since this government took office. There were also incentives to exploration and development, another program commenced by the previous government and only enlarged upon in a meagre manner by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Besources (Mr. Laing) since that time. I can sympathize with him and the difficulty he has in coping with the myopic attitudes of his cabinet colleagues in this regard. Other programs dealt with the retraining of manpower, vocational training and municipal winter works. All of these projects were the foundation for what the government is attempting to take credit for now. Devaluation of the dollar provided a tremendous impetus to Canadian exports and gave us new records in overseas trade.
All this is in danger of being thrown away on account of the unrealistic, timid and uninspired policies of this government. The Budget is an attempt simply to maintain the status quo. This is not good enough. In the affairs of men and nations, to stand still is to fall back, and where the government has not been standing still it has been leaping sideways.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And pave it too.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us hope that the
Minister of Finance has some influence on the members of the government and will be able to get them to realize that this project is one that has been long neglected and overlooked by the government which concentrates its interest on the eastern part of the country, and that the completion and paving of this highway could do a great deal for the economy not only of the west but of the whole country.
I was most interested to hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Bas-ford) classify himself as the spokesman for the four great western provinces. If he took a little closer look at things I think he would realize that the prosperity of his own province is due largely to the imaginative, impressive and progressive government of that province. Probably this is true of all the western provinces. What bothers me as I go over the Budget speech and hear the contributions to the debate made by various members is the fact that the policy of holding back or retarding the so-called economic boom in Canada comes from the federal minister in direct opposition to the over-all, sound provincial administrations across the country which I think are basically responsible for the degree of prosperity we have in Canada at this time.
The reverse ought to be true, and I think it is perhaps because of this fact that we feel we need leadership and direction from the federal government and do not have the degree of unity or national identity that we

The Budget-Mr. Thompson so desperately need. I am sure the Minister of Finance is viewing the Budget debate as a really worth-while educational experience. I hope to add a little to the debate myself.
I should like to say to the minister that I think he has made a grave mistake in stepping on the brake in an effort to control the prosperous era in our country and that he would have been much better advised to take hold of the steering wheel instead and attempt to redirect certain areas of it so that it would not end up in what could be a very undesirable situation; it is one which might be effective in some areas and completely ineffective and harmful in others. Where there is a situation of inflation, particularly in respect of the control of the spiral of prices, something needs to be done. However, Mr. Speaker, it is the contention of those of us in the Social Credit party that to apply inflationary pressures to the extent that we might burst this economic bubble is more dangerous than what the Minister of Finance is attempting to correct at the present time.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I cannot quite understand the minister as he talks about us having reached our productive capacity, because when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) gave us his guide lines in respect of United States subsidiaries operating in Canada he spoke of the need of Canadian owned companies and United States subsidiaries alike to strive for a maximum realization of the potential for full participation in the life of the Canadian economic community. To say that at this time that we have in any way reached the capacity of our productive machine is, I think, a completely false assumption because I am sure we could without any real difficulty increase our productive capacity in practically every area by 50 per cent in the next couple of years.
If the economy is operating at capacity, why is the government involved in a war on poverty? Why is the ARDA program almost swamped with requests for rehabilitation projects? Why is it that in Canada we still have
340,000	unemployed? It is not that we have a dearth of skilled labour; the fact is that we have not speeded up our retraining and educational programs nor have we applied the right incentives in the right areas to reduce this tremendously large surplus of employable labour so that the over-all picture of the economy may go forward at an even more rapid pace than is the case at the present time.
4082	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Thompson
The number of ridiculous paradoxes in our economy shows clearly that it is redirection this economy needs rather than reduced speed. We find the construction industry now having to slow down because of manpower shortages in certain areas; yet the growth in the civil service and in other governmental employment areas in Canada goes forward by leaps and bounds. We are urged to buy Canada back from the United States, but the provisions of the Bank Act make it necessary for industry and government as well to turn to the United States for the kind of risk and development capital that is needed in this country. It seems to me that Canadians are more willing to invest in the national debt because the return is higher and more secure than investing in resource development.
I think the assumption made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) yesterday, when he cried out against the so-called profiteering and gangsterism in the economic picture of this nation, is completely ill-founded, because what we need today is to encourage private Canadian capital to move into the development of Canadian resources. As evidence of this, Mr. Speaker-and I draw this point specifically to the attention of the Minister of Finance-there is the fact that Canadian borrowing on the United States market during January and February of 1966 was 11 times more than it was during those two months of 1965. Yet we learn from statistics published in the press, I think only the day before yesterday, that savings deposits in Canada amounted to nearly $10 billion at the end of February and personal savings deposits during last year increased by something like $800 million.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that what we need is redirection in a way that will encourage Canadians to invest their savings in the development of our resource wealth. Without this type of encouragement and governmental policy we have to run to the United States to obtain our capital. Those of us who believe there should be a greater degree of economic nationalism in Canada hear many people complaining about the investment of the American dollar in this country, but I do not believe this is a legitimate complaint as long as Canadians refuse to invest their savings in their own country. How can we blame someone else for investing in the resources of Canada if we apparently do not have the courage necessary to do so ourselves?

DEBATES	April 20, 1966
I believe that exports are necessary to improve our balance of payments situation, but tight money policies and taxation combine to put the Canadian producer in a non-competitive situation. In this connection I wish to refer for a few moments to the oil industry of Canada. I wonder how much concern there is on the part of Canadians with regard to the take-over of this Canadian industry by American companies, an industry which is the third largest in this country at the present time? I do not believe there is too much concern-apparently there is not -because of the reluctance of Canadians to invest in our oil industry. Even those who fear that it may eventually lead to a political take-over are cautious in their assessment of the situation. From a strictly business point of view most of them regard the capital inflow as a blessing and, in the realities of our economic life, had it not been for the willingness of Americans to invest capital in these resources they would not have been developed to the extent we see today.
I think it is an indictment of Canadian governmental policy that we have not been able to induce Canadian people to invest their savings and provide a sufficient amount of capital to develop at least half of our oil industry, and at the same time provide incentives that will encourage them to take over an even greater part of it. Without American capital where would we be in the development of our natural resources? I mention this fact only because I believe that rather than a slow-down policy or a braking of the economy there should be a redirection of the economy so that Canadians would be more willing to invest in our natural resources. Canada has had a great deal of money lying idle in savings accounts all through this development period. Billions of dollars have been lying idle. Unfortunately this has been largely caused, I believe, by the policies of the federal government, and as a result Canadians have been more interested through the years in investing in American development rather than the development of Canada.
At the present time the per capita investment in the United States by Canadians is two and a half times the per capita investment of Americans in Canada. For this reason I believe the Minister of Finance should have directed his energies and policies toward encouraging Canadians to play a greater part in the development of the resources of this country. Today the need is not to slow down production but rather to step up and
April 20, 1966

facilitate the distribution of what we can produce. One economist commented recently, "We are learning to live with prosperity, but we do not know as much about managing it as we do about getting there."
The general policy of slowing down the boom is a dangerous one. It is dangerous because the case for an inflationary situation has not really been made. The Minister of Finance says that we face the threat of dangerous inflation. I do not believe that in the traditional meaning of the word "inflation" this is true. With due respect to the attempt by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) to define "inflation," I would say the inflation to which the Minister of Finance refers, but which is not really the case is caused by too many dollars chasing too few goods. If this were the case in Canada today, why are we borrowing from the United States market the tremendous amount of money that we have borrowed for our capital development?
In the first two months of this year we borrowed from the United States market $172 million. The amount was large last year but this year there has been a general increase in borrowing from the United States. I believe that we have in Canada today not an inflationary situation but a deflationary one. I do not think we have enough capital to carry on our normal commercial and industrial activities and at the same time carry on the resource development needed in this country. What we face in Canada today is an inflation of prices. It is this inflation of prices that is causing concern all across the country. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think the general increase in prices that has been evident this year is just a beginning. It is in this area that we should be attempting to find an answer and employing the necessary slow-down in an effort to keep the cost of living in some sort of equilibrium.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The Economic Council in its second report clearly stated that there are not yet sufficient means for judging the economy to be in a phase of general inflation. The council warned the government, and I had hoped the minister would have taken more heed of this warning, by arguing that we should not be too quick to implement anti-inflationary policies. The council wisely said that fiscal and monetary policy should be aimed at sustaining economic growth over a prolonged period of time instead of using monetary policy in an attempt to control short term fluctuations
The Budget-Mr. Thompson in economic activity. Instead of attempting to slow down the entire economy, the government should have recognized the need for priority areas. In so far as expansion or maintaining the status quo is concerned, there can be no place for slowing down the productive growth of Canada. The development of our resources must go ahead with an increased rate of growth. It is the only means by which we can provide new jobs and an increased standard of living.
In this regard the attempt to apply in Canada a policy that is used in Sweden, namely, the withholding of a percentage of the earnings of corporations, I think is not going to accomplish the intended effect in any way whatever. The 5 per cent of earnings which is going to be held in a position of trust is only going to provide the security for new borrowings in foreign markets. Companies are already moving toward this idea in order to overcome the adverse effects of this particular policy. I do not believe it will work. Corporations will merely borrow on this accumulated credit.
I believe that those in this house who use Sweden as an example of the ideal controlled economy, which results in greater government control and ownership of industry, are completely wrong. The fact remains that today Sweden is basically a free enterprise country with over 90 per cent, in fact nearly 95 per cent, of her total productive machinery owned privately by the Swedish people.
I suggest to the minister there is another area of capital development which we cannot, we dare not, slow down. I am referring to essential capital development for such projects as schools, hospitals, universities and for research. We cannot slow down this type of economic development. While this is non-productive development, it is the pre-requisite for future productive development. I think the present policy of slow-down is going to run into difficulties because it is going to slow down these two areas of our economy that really should not be slowed down at all. The first one, again, is required for the productive sector of our economy and the development of our resources. The second is for the essential type of capital development which may be non-productive today but which is vitally connected with the productive process tomorrow.
There is a third area which should be considered in these areas of priority which might strictly be termed non-productive development and which could well be slowed
April 20, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Thompson down. I am speaking here of the construction of government buildings and the type of construction that is concerned with the World's Fair in Montreal as well as the centennial celebrations of our country.
This type of construction, which is truly non-productive in the sense of increasing the productive value of our economy, could well be slowed down. It could well be spread out over a longer period of time. I think what the minister should have done in his Budget was to give a new direction to the economy in these areas of priority and to have encouraged on the one hand a greater degree of expansion while on the other hand slowing down those areas that are not so much concerned with direct productive increase of the over-all economy.
In this regard it is interesting to note what is happening in connection with Expo '67. According to press reports yesterday the deficit for Expo '67 is going to be approximately $82 million, and the federal government is going to be responsible for half of that. I am not saying that construction of Expo should be slowed down, but this is the type of development that is really getting out of control. The construction of government buildings and that type of thing is all in this area as well. In fact, I think the danger that we face in Canada as a result of the Budget introduced by the minister-this is the reason I cannot agree with Budget policy-is that it will put this country into real difficulty instead of solving present problems.
There are certain areas where the expansion program is going ahead much faster than in other parts of the country. The two western provinces lead Canada in this regard, and Ontario is close behind, so far as a percentage increase is concerned. We should not be slowing that down; we should be encouraging that to go forward because that is where we are going to increase the value of our over-all economy which is going to help those areas that do not have the same increase in production.
I am concerned that the government in the Budget has seen fit to decrease the external aid program. Our external aid is not going out in the form of dollars to be spread across the world. We are using what we are able to produce and using our own personnel to help other people. This aid, therefore, comes right back to help us. I feel that this kind of aid program has some real hope of doing something big. We are using the wrong approach by reducing our aid; we should be increasing

it because it is also part of our international responsibility.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, there is another area in which the government should be applying the brake. This is the area of government expenditure as it relates to the increasing size of governments in Canada. The cost of government on the federal scene this year, along with the normal amount of supplementary estimates we can expect to be added to the proposed Budget, will bring federal expenditures into the neighbourhood of $10 billion. If we add that to the municipal and provincial budgets, we will find that in Canada today the prospect is for government expenditures to be at a level of approximately $20 billion. I do not believe we can afford this kind of luxury at this time.
I believe the Senate proposal for a basic annual income for senior citizens was the logical way for the government to help this area of our economy. The amendment to the amendment upon which we voted last night would have affected the entire structure of the economy. It was out of place at this time and therefore we could not support it.
I do believe the government should have been taking more care to slow down the increase in expenditures which have nothing to do with the productive increase in our economy. Along with this there should have been certain areas of tax reduction. I think it is interesting to note that the Alberta government has instituted a policy under which it is eliminating its share of death duties. I noted a statement in today's business section of the Gazette, in the column written by John Meyer, in which he suggests that succession duties might be one area in which we could decrease taxes and increase our own ownership of the economy.
This article says that the implementation and retention of death duties has done more to contribute to the sale of Canadian assets to foreigners than any other factor. More would be gained toward maintaining Canadian ownership by modifying these, indeed by dispensing with them altogether, than any number of Canada Development Corporations. This article refers to the differences in government about whether to go ahead with the Canada Development Corporation, and apparently these differences do exist. This type of tax reduction, I feel, would have done a great deal to speed up the productive sector of the economy instead of running the risk of slowing it down and sending this country into
April 20, 1966

another deflationary period, which I do not believe we could risk.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In this regard I also think something might have been done by the government to decrease the tremendous debt load at the present time. Last year I believe we spent $1,180 million by way of paying for the cost of our national debt. On looking at a report issued by the Tax Foundation I find that the forecast is that our national debt will increase next year at a much more rapid rate than it increased last year. This means that we are going to find ourselves involved in an ever-increasing debt load which draws capital out of productive use and throws it into that kind of dead expenditure which is the cost of government. Debt charges during the coming fiscal year will amount to approximately $60 for every man, woman and child in the country, just for the national government alone.
I suggest that had the government adopted a policy which would slow down this increase in our national debt then we might have been doing something important toward giving the right kind of direction to the economy and speeding up its productive value. I think that the government is using a monetary policy at the present time which will work in the opposite direction from that which is intended. Because of this we stand in danger, as a result of this slow-down type of budget, of pushing the country into a deflationary economic situation which we all agree we do not want. Our need in Canada is not to hold back but to move ahead. The distribution of goods and services is a field in which we are only beginning to tap our potential. Smugly we pat ourselves on the back for being good businessmen while we rationalize our own trade deficits and slow down our production.
The disposing of surplusage is a narrow and old fashioned way of assessing our tremendous production potential. What about the many other countries which do not provide their people with enough to eat? What about the vast and continuing world markets for both primary and secondary products? The time has come to institute policies to bring about a freer sale of surplus commodities and to pioneer in the field of world-wide distribution of goods from wherever they are produced to wherever they are required. This is the challenge of the age so far as the international scene and our own national economy are concerned.

The Budget-Mr. Thompson
The Globe and Mail business section of today's issue carries a series of articles which illustrate the need for clear thought and action in relation to trade. The Prime Minister of Barbados speaking yesterday in Canada said that the 1926 Canada-West Indies trade agreement is hopelessly out of date. Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce talks about the necessity of increasing our trade with the Communists behind the Iron Curtain.
What are we doing in this regard, Mr. Speaker? Are we merely gauging our trade policies in certain parts of the world on surplus commodities, or are we gearing our trade policies to the real needs of the world and our ability to meet those needs? What real efforts are being made by the government to use trade as a means of providing lasting and realistic support for developing nations? The kind of imagination and the kind of policy which we in Canada need are to be found in a policy which will not slow down in any way, or cause the government to say that they must slow down, the productive capacity of our over-all economy.
In considering the proposed amendment to the Budget motion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the amendment actually outlines the shortcomings of the policy of the Minister of Finance. Until we can aim our policies toward relieving these particular problems which are outlined in the amendment we are not going to have a satisfactory financial situation in this country.
Behind all of this is the need for bringing in a realistic monetary policy geared to the distribution of goods instead of geared to a debt system which holds back our potential productivity. We heard last night from the hon. member from Prince Edward Island about the pockets of poverty and the financial and economic situation which exists in that province, a state of affairs which can hardly be tolerated in an era of affluence such as the present. Therefore I cannot stress too strongly the danger of slowing down the economy and, instead of decreasing the cost of living or at least holding it steady, pushing ourselves into a truly deflationary period where there is not adequate capital to move what we are able to produce, with a resulting further upward spiral of living costs.
In closing I would again re-emphasize that we need to adapt our monetary policies to a greater degree of productivity and to hold back on those non-productive developments

The Budget-Mr. Leblanc which I think can be spread over a longer period of time. Such policies relate to trade, to the Bank of Canada, to the amendments which must be made to the Bank Act and to an over-all economic policy which is geared to expansion. At the same time it requires from the federal government leadership including tax reduction where necessary, bringing about an over-all production which will not just tend to hamper and to hinder the policies of some of the provinces but which will let all of the provinces work together and go forward with the type of expansion which the country needs. This is the kind of financial policy and the kind of Budget which 1 had hoped the Minister of Finance would bring down but which I do not think he has brought down. I think his present Budget will work to the detriment of the nation rather than toward the objective which he has outlined to the house.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the annual period of waiting and suspense in Canada is over since Tuesday, March 29, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) announced to the Canadian people how he intends to levy the revenues required to administer the country during the fiscal year which began on April 1.
It goes without saying that the government's receipts must be sufficient to enable it to administer the country and also to make the necessary expenditures which, in many cases, are very important incentives in the national economy.
Every year, the period preceding the bringing down of the budget is marked by temerity, anxiety, anguish, speculation and all kinds of forecasts.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Editorial writers and economists vie with each other in setting forth the reasons which, in their personal opinion, justify a relief, a stabilization or an increase of the fiscal burden.
It is obvious that no budget could ever meet with unanimous approval in a country as diversified as Canada. However, most Canadian economists and editorial writers

have praised the first budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), and I am glad to quote a few of their comments:
Ably presented document-the least partisan of all budget speeches heard in the Commons in recent years-clever innovations-appropriate budget-Mr. Sharp takes inflation seriously-expert budgetputting on the brakes-Mr. Sharp is a realist- cautious and conventional budget. If many have criticized certain measures contained in the budget, nobody rejected its general idea in order to maintain that the threat of inflation was imaginary- good doctor-in more ways than one, the Sharp budget is an act of faith.
I join with all these Canadians to commend the Minister of Finance for his courage in presenting such a budget that will ensure a continuing and progressive economic growth in this country.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, in this, my maiden speech on the budget, to briefly state to the house my concept of the relationship between government and private enterprise.
I am pleased to note that the present Liberal government favours private enterprise and provides the assistance required for complete development. Protecting private industry has always been a Liberal tenet.
One hundred or even 50 years ago, most people could live blissfully unaware of political crises in provincial or federal capitals. Today, if politics are ailing, economic and social pursuits are also affected. In the twentieth century, the state exerts a constant influence on the happiness and well-being of every businessman and individual, whereas in the nineteenth century, private initiative enjoyed complete freedom and the state simply acted as a referee between the parties.
In certain areas of the world in the twentieth century, under full socialism, private initiative is completely suppressed and taken over by the state. In Canada, our infinitely varied and mixed system must be maintained and I believe the system is perfectly justified by current economic conditions.
These days, it is not easy to find a clear and satisfactory definition of private enterprise, because under present conditions of our modern life, all economic systems are unavoidably restricted one way or another. As a rule, however, these restrictions should not, in any case, discourage private initiative or destroy freedom of action. I feel that I should quote to hon. members what His Holiness Pope John XXIII had to say about this in his encyclical Mater et Magistra. His Holiness said, and I quote:
At the outset, it should be affirmed that, in economic affairs, first place is to be given to the
April 20, 1966

private initiative of individual men who, either working by themselves, or with others in one fashion or another, pursue their common interests.
In this modern and complex world of business, it seems to me the state should co-ordinate the various forces and merely complement private enterprise, not replace it. By always echoing the claims of part of the population, it is easy for the state to forget the importance of free enterprise in the national economy. The state must not listen to the well-meaning who would like to refashion society through state intervention in economic affairs. The state must, on the contrary, fulfil with competence and dispatch its duty as legislator and, up to a point, as supervisor. The state and private enterprise must cooperate in a spirit of progress. The state must never forget that man is not made for the glorification of the state, but that the state exists for the glorification of man; and we, as legislators, must seek to bring the capitalist system to serve the whole population.
The role of the government in a competitive system, such as we have in this country, is to ensure the maintenance of conditions favourable to private initiative. To what extent the state should intervene to discourage that private initiative which made possible the economic progress all Canadians are enjoying at the present time is the big question mark.
Mr. N. R. Crump, president of the C.P.R., stated as follows at the 36th Annual Convention of the Canadian Chambers of Commerce:
Free enterprise has been the basic factor in Canadian development. Business growth, as far as the public is concerned, may be due to the particular situation of Canada as compared to other countries. For a country which had no future either economically (because of American inducements) or politically (because of a diffuseness inherent in bilingualism and biculturalism), Canada, nevertheless, accomplished some remarkable achievements.
The Canadian government should, with foresight, establish a clear economic policy creating a climate favourable to investments. It should stimulate, co-ordinate and develop the sense of responsibilities, the love of work and savings, but never try to absorb or destroy creative energy and the sense of responsibilities. In North America, as you know, private enterprise created the highest standard of living in the world, even if it has not yet completely eliminated poverty and unemployment; and Canada, like the United States, should be a bulwark of private enterprise.
Suggested National Indian Day
Therefore, it must set up a list of priority for its expenditures in order to ensure its participation in the improvement of the competitive situation in our Canadian economy, because its initiatives and its legislation affect the whole population; it can have a determining effect on our industrial expansion, by using wisely its tremendous purchasing power.
The state must co-operate with the public and private sectors. It must exercise a wise control, based on the general interest and with the experience of the private sector, in order to make its initiatives more dynamic and efficient. I have confidence in the type of co-operation which has always existed in Canada between government and private enterprise, and I earnestly hope to see the continuation of this type of co-operation, so that our country may attain full economical development. The government must continue to assist our industry in order to create activities liable to bring about other satellite activities. It must continue to promote the expansion of Canadian enterprise through an acceleration of its program of industrial research and its program of services for technical consultations. It must also continue to use the tax factor.
You will all agree with me when I say that the intervention of the state is obvious, at the present time, but that such intervention must necessarily be restricted to areas and a method of operation-
